title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: Scalability
summary: Scalability is the ability of a system to handle growing load — more requests, more data, more users — by adding resources, ideally in a way where throughput increases roughly linearly with the resources added.
objectives: Define vertical scaling and horizontal scaling, and give one workload best suited to each.
What does "linear scaling" mean and how do you detect sub-linear scaling?
Why is the first rule of horizontal scaling "make services stateless"?
Explain the scalability staircase and why the order matters.

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Scalability is the ability of a system to handle growing load — more requests, more data, more users — by adding resources, ideally in a way where throughput increases roughly linearly with the resources added.

Scalability is the most-asked NFR in system design interviews, and it is also the most often misunderstood. A system is scalable if, when you double the resources you give it, throughput roughly doubles and per-request latency stays flat. If throughput rises only 1.3x when you double the hardware, the system is scaling sub-linearly and a bottleneck exists somewhere — a lock, a shared resource, a single primary, a connection pool. If throughput does not rise at all, the system is not scalable; it is just bigger. The discipline of scalability engineering is identifying and removing those bottlenecks until adding resources buys proportional capacity. There are two fundamental strategies — vertical scaling (scale up) and horizontal scaling (scale out) — and almost every real architecture is a blend of both, chosen per layer based on the kind of bottleneck present.

**Vertical scaling** means making a single machine bigger: more CPU, more RAM, faster disks, a larger network pipe. It is the simplest form of scaling because the application code does not change — you just run it on a more powerful box. Vertical scaling works beautifully until it doesn't. The ceiling is the largest instance your cloud provider offers (today, roughly a few hundred vCPUs and several terabytes of RAM on AWS bare-metal). Beyond that you cannot go. Vertical scaling is also a single point of failure: if your one big box dies, your whole system dies. And it has poor cost curve — the largest instance typically costs 8–10x a mid-size instance while delivering only 4–5x the throughput, because vendors price scarcity. Vertical scaling is the right answer when the workload is single-threaded and stateful, or when the team is small and operational simplicity matters more than theoretical limits. In-memory caches like Redis primaries are often vertically scaled: a single huge Redis node with hundreds of gigabytes of RAM outperforms a cluster for many workloads and avoids the complexity of cross-slot operations.

**Horizontal scaling** means adding more machines and distributing load across them. It is the only strategy with no theoretical ceiling — you can keep adding nodes until you run out of money. But horizontal scaling is hard because it requires the workload to be **partitionable** (each request can be handled by any node, or by a specific node determined by a sharding key) and the nodes to be either **stateless** (so any node can serve any request) or **stateful with explicit sharding** (so each node owns a slice of the data). Stateless services are easy to scale horizontally: put a load balancer in front, add instances, drain unhealthy ones. Stateful services are hard: shards must be balanced, resharding must not drop writes, and cross-shard operations must be reasoned about carefully. This is why the first commandment of horizontal scaling is "make services stateless" — push session state, file uploads, and shared mutable data into dedicated stores (Redis, S3, a database) so the compute tier can be cloned freely.

The bottleneck hierarchy, often called the **scalability staircase**, dictates where to scale next. Load enters at the load balancer, hits the web tier, then the application tier, then the cache, then the database. You scale whichever tier is saturated first. If the web tier hits 80% CPU, add web nodes. If the database primary is CPU-bound, add read replicas for read traffic and consider sharding for write traffic. If the cache is evicting heavily, add cache nodes or increase the working-set hit rate. If the network pipe is saturated, upgrade the pipe or move to a CDN. A common mistake is to scale one tier past the point of diminishing returns while another tier is the actual bottleneck — for example, adding 50 web nodes when the single database primary is the limit. Measurement must precede scaling.

Real-world example: Netflix's transition from vertical scaling in owned data centers to horizontal autoscaling on AWS. In the late 2000s Netflix ran on vertically-scaled Oracle databases and big-iron servers in their own DCs. They hit two walls simultaneously: traffic was growing faster than they could procure and rack hardware, and a single DC was a single point of failure (a flood or power loss would take the whole service down). The move to AWS in 2008–2010 was fundamentally a move from vertical to horizontal scaling — instead of buying one bigger box, Netflix ran hundreds of smaller instances behind autoscaling groups. The pattern generalized: stateless web and API tiers autoscale on CPU; stateful tiers (Cassandra, EVCache) are sharded; batch and encoding workloads autoscale on queue depth. The benefit was not just capacity but resilience — losing an instance became a non-event, handled by an autoscaler rather than a human. The cost was operational complexity: Netflix had to invent chaos engineering (the Simian Army) to verify the horizontally-scaled system actually survived instance failures.

A second real-world example, this time from Redis internals. A single Redis instance is vertically scaled — one thread, one process, one machine. To scale horizontally, Redis introduced Cluster mode, which shards keys across nodes using a hash slot (16,384 slots total). Each node owns a contiguous range of slots, and resharding moves slots between nodes without downtime. The trade-off is explicit: multi-key operations only work when all keys map to the same slot, so application developers must encode the shard key into the key (e.g., `user:{42}:cart` and `user:{42}:profile` are guaranteed to live on the same node). This is the canonical pattern for sharding stateful systems — the cost of horizontal scale is borne by the application, which must know its shard key up front.

Pitfalls are everywhere. **Premature sharding** — sharding a database at 1K QPS because someone read a blog post — adds operational pain for no benefit; you should shard when the largest single primary cannot keep up, not before. **Ignoring the bottleneck** — adding web nodes when the database is saturated — wastes money. **Stateful services pretending to be stateless** — a service that caches session state in process memory but is fronted by a round-robin LB will randomly log users out, a bug that surfaces only under load. **Cross-shard transactions** — trying to maintain ACID across shards — is the graveyard of distributed-systems designs; use sagas or eventual consistency instead. **Autoscaling lag** — autoscalers react to past metrics, so a 10x spike will still overload the fleet for 2–5 minutes before new nodes warm up; you need warm spare capacity or predictive scaling, not pure reactive scaling.

Scalability connects to almost every other phase. Caching (Phase 4) is the cheapest form of read scaling. Load balancing (Phase 5) is the mechanism that distributes horizontal scale. Message queues (Phase 7) decouple producers from consumers so each can scale independently. Sharded databases (Phase 3) and microservices (Phase 8) are architectural patterns that enable horizontal scale. Observability (Phase 11) is what tells you which tier is the bottleneck. The art of scalable design is choosing, for each layer, the right mix of vertical and horizontal scaling, and resisting the urge to scale a tier past its actual bottleneck.

```mermaid
    CACHE -->|miss| PRIMARY[(DB Primary)]
    R1 <--> PRIMARY

```

### ASCII Diagram
```
                       Vertical scaling
                       = bigger box
                       +------------------+
                       | 1 machine, 64 CPU|
                       | 1 TB RAM, NVMe   |
                       +------------------+
                              (ceiling: largest instance)

                       Horizontal scaling
                       = more boxes
            +--------+   +--------+   +--------+
            | node 1 |   | node 2 |   | node N |
            +--------+   +--------+   +--------+
                \            |            /
                 +-----------+-----------+
                             |
                          load balancer
                  (ceiling: ~ money + ops)
```

### Walkthrough
1. Measure per-tier saturation (CPU, memory, connection pool, disk I/O, network). The first tier to cross ~70% utilization is the bottleneck.
2. If the bottleneck is stateless (web/API), scale horizontally — add instances behind a load balancer. If it is stateful (database primary), first scale reads via replicas, then scale writes via sharding.
3. Re-measure after each scaling move; the bottleneck will move. Repeat until throughput scales linearly with added resources or until cost becomes the constraint.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# A toy autoscaler that simulates CPU-based scale-out for a stateless
# service. Illustrates the reactive-autoscaling loop used by Kubernetes
# HorizontalPodAutoscaler, AWS Auto Scaling Groups, etc.

import random
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List

@dataclass
class Instance:
    id: int
    cpu: float = 0.0          # 0..1 utilization
    healthy: bool = True

@dataclass
class Autoscaler:
    min_size: int
    max_size: int
    target_cpu: float         # scale-out if avg cpu > target
    scale_in_factor: float    # scale-in if avg cpu < target * factor
    cooldown_s: int           # seconds between scaling decisions
    instances: List[Instance] = field(default_factory=list)
    next_id: int = 0
    last_action_s: int = -10_000

    def __post_init__(self):
        for _ in range(self.min_size):
            self._add()

    def _add(self):
        self.instances.append(Instance(id=self.next_id))
        self.next_id += 1

    def _remove(self, idx: int):
        self.instances[idx].healthy = False
        self.instances.pop(idx)

    def avg_cpu(self) -> float:
        if not self.instances:
            return 0.0
        return sum(i.cpu for i in self.instances) / len(self.instances)

    def tick(self, t: int, incoming_qps: int):
        # Step 1: distribute load evenly across healthy instances
        n = max(1, len(self.instances))
        per_node = incoming_qps / n
        # cpu is roughly linear in per-node qps up to a saturation point
        for inst in self.instances:
            inst.cpu = min(1.0, per_node / 500.0 + random.uniform(-0.03, 0.03))

        # Step 2: respect cooldown
        if t - self.last_action_s < self.cooldown_s:
            return

        # Step 3: scale-out decision
        if self.avg_cpu() > self.target_cpu and len(self.instances) < self.max_size:
            n_add = max(1, int((self.avg_cpu() - self.target_cpu) * len(self.instances)))
            for _ in range(n_add):
                self._add()
            self.last_action_s = t
            print(f"t={t:4d}  scale OUT  +{n_add}  -> {len(self.instances)} "
                  f"(avg_cpu={self.avg_cpu():.2f}, qps={incoming_qps})")
        # Step 4: scale-in decision
        elif self.avg_cpu() < self.target_cpu * self.scale_in_factor \
                and len(self.instances) > self.min_size:
            n_rm = max(1, len(self.instances) // 4)
            for _ in range(n_rm):
                self._remove(0)
            self.last_action_s = t
            print(f"t={t:4d}  scale IN   -{n_rm}  -> {len(self.instances)} "
                  f"(avg_cpu={self.avg_cpu():.2f}, qps={incoming_qps})")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asg = Autoscaler(min_size=3, max_size=20, target_cpu=0.6,
                     scale_in_factor=0.5, cooldown_s=60)
    # Simulate 30 minutes (1800s) sampled every 60s with a viral spike
    qps_schedule = [1000]*5 + [3000, 6000, 8000, 10000, 9000,
                               7000, 5000, 3000, 2000, 1500] + [1000]*11
    for t, qps in enumerate(qps_schedule, start=0):
        asg.tick(t*60, qps)
```

quiz.explanation: Linear scaling means throughput grows in proportion to resources added — double the nodes, double the QPS at the same latency. Sub-linear scaling means throughput grows slower than resources — double the nodes, get only 1.3x QPS — because a bottleneck remains.

quiz.explanation: A stateless service can serve any request on any instance, so a load balancer can freely add, remove, and rebalance instances — that is the foundation of horizontal autoscaling. A stateful service cannot: if instance A holds user 42's session, every request from user 42 must reach instance A (sticky sessions) or the state must be replicated to all instances (expensive and inconsistent).

quiz.question: Explain the scalability staircase and why the order matters.
options: Low CPU but high latency points to a non-CPU bottleneck — most likely a downstream resource the web tier is waiting on.
The root cause is autoscaling lag combined with insufficient headroom — the architecture was sized for steady-state, not for spikes.

quiz.explanation: The scalability staircase is the order in which tiers saturate as load grows: load balancer → web tier → app tier → cache → database primary (writes) → database replicas (reads) → network egress. You scale whichever tier is currently the bottleneck; scaling a non-bottleneck tier wastes money.
